_comment: Readings taken off the manufacturer's reference calculator. This is the ONLY
check in dev/replay.mjs that can confirm accuracy rather than self-consistency.
The original ~43 readings behind the Duplex constants were never stored - they
survive only as prose in the source comments, and that prose has drifted: the
0.2625/0.2253 note still quotes x = 15.597 / 15.265, which no drum reproduces
with the C the code now holds. The underlying readings were recoverable in that
one case because the note also gave the resulting lengths, which bracket C. Most
notes do not, and those readings are gone.
status 'verified' - full inputs and expected outputs; replay.mjs asserts it.
status 'partial'  - recorded from a comment but missing inputs (usually the
drum). NOT asserted. This is the re-measurement worklist.
Add readings with: node dev/worklist.mjs   (see dev/README.md)

readings.source: Reference calculator API response, supplied by the user 2026-10-01. Inputs pinned by the returned multiplier and TIPPT.
note: LENGTH CONFIRMS THE CATALOG FORMULA. active = 1 x 2463.10 / 136.7855 =
18.005 -> 18, with no fitted constant. The old fitted C gave 18.4507 and
the old rule then added 0.25", for 18.25".
The reference's own spring weights confirm the lengths independently:
STEEL_DENSITY x (pi^2/4) x wire x (ID + wire) x L reproduces 13.2669 and
26.8447 to four decimals at L = 18 and 19 exactly.
referenceCycles is recorded but NOT asserted: the duplex cycle model is
still unresolved. Inverting the reference's own counts needs 3-5% more
inner-spring torque than the physical active length produces, and no
single factor reconciles all six readings (the implied ratio runs 1.003
to 1.056). The field is confirmed to be computed life, not the target
echoed back: 585 lb returns 12,000 against a 10,000 target.

readings.source: Reference calculator API response, supplied by the user 2026-10-01. Inputs pinned by the returned multiplier and TIPPT.
note: THE ONE READING THE PHYSICAL FORMULA DOES NOT REPRODUCE, and the only one
with a fractional length. Marked 'divergent' so replay.mjs records it
without asserting it.
The reference REJECTS this design itself: status 'warning', 'cycle life
calculation of 1,165,000.00 exceeds the 350,000 cycle maximum'.
It also contradicts itself here. Inverting its own reported cycle count
gives a body length of 34.773, which agrees with the catalog formula's
34.875 to 0.3% - while it prints 36.25. So its internal arithmetic uses
the same active length everything else does, and only the PRINTED length
differs. Until that is understood, fitting the general rule to this
reading is what produced the tau regime in the first place.
Both wires are also at or near their minimum for their spring ID (0.2253
is exactly the published minimum for 3 3/4"), so the design is pinned at
the soft end of the ladder and cannot step down.

readings.source: Comment on the 0.2730/0.2253 entry: 'Two readings (600 lb at 7'0", 572 lb at 11'2")'. Drum, spring count, radius and target not recorded, and no length given, so nothing can be asserted.
Comment on the 0.2830/0.2343 entry: three readings at 683 lb, at 11'2", 11'0" and 9'0", used to pin tau to 20.25-21.25. Lengths not recorded.

Comment on the 0.2890/0.2343 entry: the 726/727 lb pair either side of the reference's own accept/reject line at 11'0", which brackets K to within 4. The most valuable reading type described anywhere in the file - a boundary - and the inputs behind it were not kept.
Reference calculator API response, supplied by the user 2026-10-01.
note: NOW REPRODUCED. This reading was marked divergent while the quarter inch was
unexplained. With the three-regime thresholds fitted from this rung's own
9-point sweep it comes out exactly, length and weights.
THE QUARTER INCH IS REAL, and this reading proves it. 16.25", straight
from the API, on an in-range design the reference does not complain about.
It also vindicates the old source comment, which claimed exactly 16.25" at
460 lb and 15.00" at 470 lb. That comment was briefly marked superseded
here on the grounds that its quoted x values no longer reproduced - the x
values were stale, but the LENGTHS it reported were right.
WHAT THE FORMULA GIVES: active = 2 x 1014.75 / 133.875 = 15.158, which
rounds to 15. The reference says 16.25, so this is +1.09 out.
THE 460/470 PAIR IS THE SHARPEST EVIDENCE IN THE FILE. Same drum, same
height, same spring count, same wires, 10 lb apart - and the reference
steps 16.25" -> 15", a drop of 1.25", where the active length moves only
0.32". That is a genuine quantisation, not rounding, and no smooth
function of the active length reproduces it.
Both quarter-inch readings so far (this and 200 lb) are on the SOFTEST
pairing, 0.2625/0.2253, where the inner wire sits exactly at its
published minimum for 3 3/4" and cannot step down.

readings.source: Reference calculator API response, supplied by the user 2026-10-01, as part of a TARGET SWEEP on one door: 470 lb, 1 spring, 7'0", D400-144, radius 15. TIPPT 136.8 and turns 7.9 are identical across the whole sweep, so only the target varies - which is what makes these the cleanest available test of the cycle model.
note: FOUR NEW PAIRINGS came out of this sweep - 0.3625/0.289, 0.3938/0.3065,
0.3938/0.3195 and 0.4062/0.331 - none of them in DUPLEX_PAIRS. All four fall
inside duplexPairBalanced's stress window, which is independent confirmation
of that rule: 7 of 7 sweep pairings are in the window.
IT ALSO CONTRADICTS DUPLEX_CATALOGUE, which claims a 50,000 target tops out
at S = 5920. The reference used S = 8723 at exactly that target. Since S
depends only on the two wire sizes, a product catalogue cannot depend on
spring count - yet at 2 springs the cap makes this very pairing unreachable.

readings.source: Reference calculator API response, user-supplied 2026-10-01. Part of a DENSE WEIGHT SWEEP: 440-480 lb in 5 lb steps, 2 springs, 7'0", D400-144, radius 15, target 10,000. One pairing (0.2625/0.2253) throughout, so only the active length varies - the cleanest test of the length rule anywhere in this file.
note: THE SWEEP IS NON-MONOTONIC IN WEIGHT, which is the whole finding:
wt   TIPPT   active    frac    reference L
A HEAVIER DOOR GETS A LONGER SPRING at 445->450 and again at 475->480. No
monotonic function of the active length can do that, so the quarter inch is
a genuine quantisation and not rounding.
ON THIS PAIRING the rule that fits all nine is:
frac(active) ~ 0        ->  L = round(active)
0.01 < frac < ~0.6      ->  L = ceil(active) + 0.25
frac > ~0.6             ->  L = ceil(active)
tau bracketed between frac 0.5290 (gets the quarter) and 0.6734 (does not).
BUT IT DOES NOT GENERALISE, and that is why it is not implemented. Six
readings on OTHER pairings have frac in the 0.01-0.6 band and take NO
those plain round(active) is exact. So the quarter belongs to this pairing,
or to something about it not yet identified - note it is the SOFTEST rung on
the ladder, and the out-of-range 200 lb anomaly is on it too.
Implementing an unexplained per-pairing regime is exactly what produced the
tau constant that this work removed, and tau is why no drum but the D400-144
ever came out right. Characterised here rather than coded.

readings.source: Reference API, user-supplied 2026-10-01. SECOND DENSE SWEEP: 560-600 lb in 5 lb steps, 2 springs, 7'0", target 10,000 - landing on the 0.273/0.2253 pairing throughout. Taken specifically to test whether the quarter-inch regime is pairing-specific. It is not.
note: THE QUARTER INCH IS NOT PAIRING-SPECIFIC. 575 lb returns 14.25" on
0.273/0.2253, so the hypothesis that it belonged to the softest rung alone
is dead - and implementing it scoped to that rung, which was the other
option on the table, would have been wrong.
wt   TIPPT   active    frac    refL   floor+
WHAT THE TWO SWEEPS TOGETHER PROVE. Both show the SAME three-regime
structure, in the same order as frac(active) falls:
frac >= tHi        ->  floor(active) + 1
tLo <= frac < tHi  ->  floor(active) + 1.25
frac <  tLo        ->  floor(active)
and with thresholds fitted per pairing it reproduces all 18 readings exactly:
NO SINGLE THRESHOLD PAIR CAN SERVE BOTH, and this is a proof rather than a
failure to find one: sweep 1 requires frac 0.158-0.529 to give +1.25 while

readings.source: Reference API, user-supplied 2026-10-01. Taken to test a predicted 15.25" at 680/685 lb; the prediction turned out to be for the wrong rung (see note).
note: THE 90% ACCEPTANCE RULE - the most important thing these three readings show.
680 lb returns 10,000 on 0.283/0.2343 and 685 lb returns 9,000 on the SAME
rung with status 'warning'. At 690 lb it steps to 0.289/0.2343. That is the
second such boundary: 725 lb does exactly the same on 0.289/0.2343 before
stepping to 0.295 at 730.
Both boundaries sit at 9,000 against a 10,000 target - exactly 0.90. So the
reference accepts the softest rung reaching about 90% of target and WARNS
below 100%, rather than requiring the target outright. That is the behaviour
the source comments have described since the first commit as 'takes a
combination that does not reach the target'.
CONFIRMED A THIRD WAY, from the reference's own data and with no reliance on
this app's K: 620 lb measures 14,000 cycles on 0.283/0.2253. Scaling to 680
lb by the cycle law alone, 14,000 / (680/620)^4.67 = 9,000 - right on the
boundary. So at 680 lb that rung falls to 90% and the reference steps off it,
which is precisely what it does.
WHY THE RULE IS NOT IMPLEMENTED. Scored over 27 readings, loosening the
threshold makes the wire choice WORSE, not better:
The rule is right and the model still gets worse with it, because a lower
threshold lets MORE rungs qualify and so amplifies every error in K. At 680
lb this app thinks 0.283/0.2253 still clears the target when the reference's
own numbers put it at 9,000. The strict f = 1.00 currently in use is
compensating for optimistic K values.
That makes three compensating errors now identified - the strict threshold,
DUPLEX_CATALOGUE's cap, and the pessimistic kSlope line - each of which
measures worse when fixed alone. K has to be fixed first.
ON THE FAILED PREDICTION: 15.25" was predicted for 680/685 on the assumption
they would land on 0.289/0.2343. They land on 0.283/0.2343, so the band
computed was for the wrong rung and the three-regime length model was NOT
tested. On the rung they did use, active is 13.855 and 13.751, frac 0.855 and
0.751, both giving floor+1 - consistent with the model, not decisive for it.

which is precisely what it does.
WHY THE RULE IS NOT IMPLEMENTED. Scored over 27 readings, loosening the
threshold makes the wire choice WORSE, not better:
The rule is right and the model still gets worse with it, because a lower
threshold lets MORE rungs qualify and so amplifies every error in K. At 680
lb this app thinks 0.283/0.2253 still clears the target when the reference's
own numbers put it at 9,000. The strict f = 1.00 currently in use is
compensating for optimistic K values.
That makes three compensating errors now identified - the strict threshold,
DUPLEX_CATALOGUE's cap, and the pessimistic kSlope line - each of which
measures worse when fixed alone. K has to be fixed first.
ON THE FAILED PREDICTION: 15.25" was predicted for 680/685 on the assumption
they would land on 0.289/0.2343. They land on 0.283/0.2343, so the band
computed was for the wrong rung and the three-regime length model was NOT
tested. On the rung they did use, active is 13.855 and 13.751, frac 0.855 and
0.751, both giving floor+1 - consistent with the model, not decisive for it.

readings.source: Reference API, user-supplied 2026-10-01. DRUM VERIFICATION set: every other reading in this file is on the D400-144, so these six test whether removing tau really made the model drum-independent. Predictions were published before the readings were taken.
note: WIRE CHOICE WAS 6/6 ACROSS BOTH OTHER DRUMS, which closes the original
complaint that the calculator 'sucks for any drum that isn't 400-144'.
The D525-216's rEff is 28% above the D400s' and that is exactly what the
old tau threshold could not survive; with tau gone there is nothing left
that can be drum-specific, and these readings confirm it.
LENGTH WAS 4/6. Both misses are frac(active) near 0.6 on rungs that have
no fitted thresholds, so round(active) rounds up where the reference
floors. That is the known quarter-inch gap, not a drum problem - and
these two readings are what finally bound those rungs' tLo.
